newsitem.title: USA: Possible tobacco settlement shadows Miami court.
newsitem.headline: Possible tobacco settlement shadows Miami court.

text.p: Washington talks on a tobacco settlement shadowed a Miami courtroom Thursday as attorneys selected jurors for a landmark suit that legal experts said could be cut short by an industry deal with states to wipe out anti-tobacco litigation.

Norma Broin, the American Airlines flight attendant whose bout with lung cancer prompted her to become lead plaintiff in the case, said she was angry at politicians and even health care organisations involved in the talks, which she viewed as denying her and others the chance to obtain relief.
"I am just so opposed, very, very, very opposed ... These people deserve a day in court. It's just not right," she said.

On Monday, Dade County, Fla., Circuit Judge Robert Kaye indicated that he did not expect a settlement to affect the case, known as Norma Broin vs. Philip Morris Cos. Inc., the first class action suit and first second-hand smoke suit to make it to trial.

"We will proceed as we are proceeding, and we will continue until someone convinces me otherwise," Kaye said. He also said he could foresee "very serious" constitutional problems if federal judges or officials attempted to stop a state case already underway as part of a nationwide settlement.

Kaye stopped short of adhering to a request by the plaintiffs' attorneys, Stanley and Susan Rosenblatt, who have not been involved in the settlement talks, that he formally state that the action would not be stalled by a settlement pact.

The Broin suit was filed in 1991 on behalf of thousands of non-smoking flight attendants seeking as much as $5 billion in damages from tobacco firms for illnesses they attribute to breathing second-hand cigarette smoke on passenger jets.

After years of legal manoeuvring, it made it to court this month after the Rosenblatts, who say the class would include as many as 60,000 flight attendants, spent $500,000 in the process of preparing the case to trial.

Tobacco industry attorneys in Miami for the suit said they were not privy to the details of the talks between industry officials and state attorneys general seeking to recoup the health care costs of smokers.
"I can only say we intend to try this lawsuit on the merits," said David Hardy, who represents Philip Morris and Lorillard Inc.
State officials and cigarette makers began negotiating in early April to resolve massive litigation in exchange for funding of personal injury claims and public health concessions.

Thursday afternoon, Mississippi Attorney General Mike Moore, the chief negotiator for the states in talks with cigarette companies, said tremendous progress had been made toward a settlement, but no announcement of an agreement was likely Thursday.

Legal experts said it was difficult to say whether a federal settlement could actually stop the Broin case. They also said the case almost certainly would not be affected by a settlement if a judgment were reached before an agreement were finalised.

But that seemed unlikely. By late afternoon Thursday, the 11th day of jury selection, attorneys had picked 66 potential jurors, who will form the pool from which a panel of six and 10 alternates will be selected. The final pool is expected to include about 100.
The trial is expected to last as long as three months after jury selection is finished.
